intro: Zeroing random activations also changes their average magnitude. This activity supplies the mask so you can study the scaling rule without guessing which random numbers were drawn.
task: Return a NumPy array equal to x * keep / (1-p) during training and an unchanged-value copy of x during evaluation. Here p is the probability of dropping an entry; keep is a supplied boolean mask, not a probability.
requirements: x is a nonempty array with at least one axis. keep has exactly the same shape and boolean dtype; True means keep.
p is a finite scalar with 0 <= p < 1. training must be a Python bool. Reject malformed inputs with ValueError, including during evaluation.
Require finite x. Do not generate random numbers or infer p from how many entries are True in this particular mask.
Do not modify inputs or return an alias of x. A supplied mask is applied literally during training, even when p is zero. Checks use moderate values and p away from one.

hints.title: Name the probability
hints.body: p is the chance of dropping. The chance of keeping is 1-p, which belongs in the denominator.

hints.title: Do not estimate the keep rate
hints.body: A small random mask need not have exactly its expected fraction of True values. Use the supplied p.

hints.title: Test the expectation
hints.body: For one input value with p=0.5, average the two equally likely masks [True] and [False].

explanation: A Bernoulli keep mask is one with probability 1-p. Dividing a kept activation by 1-p makes the expected training output equal to the input.

The supplied mask makes this lesson deterministic. A real dropout layer samples masks, but the scaling is based on the distribution's keep probability rather than the observed fraction kept in one batch.
Evaluation returns the input values because the training-time rescaling already accounts for missing activations. This is the inverted-dropout convention.

Compare a mask that keeps every entry with one that drops every entry. Neither outcome invalidates the expectation rule: it describes an average over random masks, not every individual pass. The expectation statement assumes masks are sampled with the stated probability.
formula: train(x) = x ⊙ keep / (1 − p); eval(x) = x
